title: Workflow and Task Structure Redesign
summary: Creative Navy uses workflow and task structure redesign to investigate how work is actually done, decompose tasks before design decisions are made, and restructure interfaces around real operating sequences, handoffs, dependencies, and role-specific needs. The evidence includes field-measured, client-measured, client-reported, and design-only cases with different levels of confidence.
keyFacts: Workflow analysis and task analysis investigate how work is actually done, not how it is supposed to be done.
Task structure and task sequence refer to the ordering and grouping of discrete actions within a workflow.
Microtask analysis documents discrete user actions independently of assumed sequence or flow to reveal cognitive load structure.
Triopsis mapped 47 microtasks across 3 personas before design decisions were made.
Triopsis research included 43 user interviews, 21 participants, and 3 in-situ observation sessions under real operational pressure.
Beissbarth calibration time changed from 18 to 12 minutes per vehicle, client-measured across 8 production deployment locations.
MSolutions' key diagnostic workflow changed from 26 interactions to approximately 13, client-reported from internal task walkthroughs.
Gexcon documented 102 individual tasks across the full simulation workflow.
Topera was a concept design only; nothing has been built and no outcome is claimed.
Egma Order is live, but no post-launch measurement is stated.

bodySections.heading: Definition and Scope of Workflow and Task Structure Redesign
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Workflow and task structure redesign is the structured analysis and redesign of task ordering, task grouping, handoff points, dependencies, role coordination, abnormal states, and non-linear work patterns within complex software workflows.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method uses workflow analysis, task analysis, and microtask analysis to expose where users need sequence, where users need random access, where roles diverge, where handoffs fail, and where abnormal workflow states are routine operating conditions rather than edge cases.

bodySections.heading: When Workflow and Task Structure Redesign Is Needed
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow and task structure redesign is needed when the interface sequence does not match the sequence of work. This can appear as a backend-module interface that does not match a diagnostic procedure, a wizard that hides prior decisions users must revise, or a dashboard that presents information before users have answered the questions that determine their next action.

Workflow and task structure redesign is needed in multi-role systems. In the Triopsis workforce management case, schedulers, operations managers, and field technicians had incompatible mental models inside one system. Schedulers needed speed, batch actions, and team availability. Operations managers needed exception scanning and a broader time horizon. Field technicians needed task detail, safety compliance, and support for outdoor conditions.

Workflow and task structure redesign is also needed when abnormal states are normal operating conditions. In Triopsis, in-situ observation showed schedulers handling weather incidents, conflicting locations, overlapping jobs, and sudden crew shortages. These conditions were treated as part of the real workflow that the interface had to support.

Workflow and task structure redesign is needed when expert work is non-linear. In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, engineers moved between scenario setup, parameter configuration, visualisation, and validation in sequences that depended on what they found at each stage. The workflow could not be represented as one fixed sequence.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy Analyses Workflow and Task Structure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy treats existing workflows as evidence. Existing workflows encode what an interface has been asked to do, including failure modes, hidden dependencies, workarounds, and capabilities worth preserving. Analysing the workflow before redesign makes the operating structure visible before screens, navigation, or visual hierarchy are settled.

Microtask analysis decomposes work into discrete user actions independently of an assumed screen flow. In Triopsis, 47 microtasks were mapped across 3 personas before design decisions were made. For each microtask, Creative Navy recorded when it was performed, ease of discovery, ease of understanding, user needs, issues, opportunities, desired outcome, pain points, patterns, frequency, cognitive load, and dependencies.

Task analysis can also be used for complex expert workflows. In Gexcon, 102 individual tasks were documented across the full simulation workflow, including goals, frequency, difficulty, actions, and hierarchy of needs within sequences. The redesign then created explicit requirements for significant interactions, including purpose, constraints, dependencies, expected behaviour, values that had to remain visible during scenario setup, warning placement, and system response to incomplete input.

bodySections.heading: What Workflow and Task Structure Redesign Produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow and task structure redesign produces task sequences that reflect real work order. In Beissbarth automotive calibration, the workflow had to support a sequential and timing-sensitive procedure while technicians moved around the vehicle with tools in hand and depended on unambiguous feedback from three distinct interfaces. The design decision was that the workflow is the interface: each screen communicates the next action rather than asking the technician to navigate to find functions.

Workflow and task structure redesign produces role-specific visibility where one system serves different operational contexts. In Triopsis, microtask decomposition showed that improving one role's workflow created blind spots for another role. This was a structural organisational tension made visible through task decomposition, not a simple design error.

Workflow and task structure redesign produces dependency-aware structures. In Topera, a concept design for a cross-organisational project management platform grounded in the DIN 69901 series, project definition was designed as a single long working page rather than a wizard. The design included left navigation with per-area completion state, a central working column, and a right panel carrying settings, recommendations, and contextual validation.

Workflow and task structure redesign can also produce explicit gates. In Topera, the transition out of the DIN 69901-2 Definition phase was designed as a phase clearance checklist enumerating each area and its state, identifying incomplete and blocked items, and providing a submission action for review and clearance into the DIN 69901-2 Planning phase.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Redesign in Multi-Role and Operational-Pressure Systems
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Triopsis workforce management case shows workflow redesign in a multi-role operational system. Creative Navy mapped 47 microtasks across schedulers, operations managers, and field technicians, supported by 43 user interviews, 21 participants, and 3 in-situ observation sessions under real operational pressure. The in-situ observation revealed behaviour under pressure that interview self-report did not surface.

The Triopsis field technician compliance component surfaced required steps at the right moment in the workflow, highlighted dependencies, and showed safety requirements without overloading technicians working outdoors under time pressure.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Redesign in Sequential, Diagnostic, and Expert Systems
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Beissbarth automotive calibration case shows workflow redesign in a sequential, timing-sensitive, multi-device procedure. Technicians moved around the vehicle with tools in hand and relied on unambiguous feedback from three distinct interfaces. The workflow had to support the calibration procedure as a coherent sequence that did not pause for interface interpretation.

The MSolutions AV diagnostic instruments case shows workflow redesign as diagnostic narrative. The previous design organised screens by backend modules, and two prior redesigns had addressed the visual layer without correcting that structural mismatch. The audit named the mismatch, and the workflow redesign followed the diagnostic sequence rather than the backend structure.

The Gexcon CFD simulation case shows workflow redesign in a complex expert workflow. The workflow was non-linear: engineers moved between scenario setup, parameter configuration, visualisation, and validation depending on what they discovered at each stage.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Redesign in Inspection, Information-Consumption, and Financial Workflows
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The WCO/IPM case involved inspection and enforcement workflows across 107 governments. Three user groups had distinct workflow types: officers performed time-pressured inspection against alerts, analysts performed pattern analysis and case building, and rights holders filed and monitored cases. The workflow analysis rebuilt the information architecture around real inspection and case management flows rather than internal system structures.

WCO/IPM applied cognitive design principles to workflow: recognition over recall, reduced choices per screen, progressive disclosure, and contextual micro-hints on first use of complex actions. The case records that parallel spreadsheets and email chains disappeared when the platform workflows were redesigned to support what people were actually doing.

Chemical Watch shows information consumption as workflow. User research found that compliance professionals consume regulatory news chronologically as a professional practice of staying current. Breaking chronological order created anxiety about whether obligations had been covered. The lens view was redesigned as a workspace: a persistent, named, configured view that users returned to as part of their regular workflow.

The Dancerace / Jacko invoice management portal connected financier, supplier, and debtor workflows. Research found a strict internal priority order: users needed to answer what they owed, what their cost was, and what tasks they had to do immediately before they could act on anything else. That hierarchy of needs determined the workflow architecture.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Redesign in Assembly Planning, Project Definition, B2B Ordering, and Industrial Automation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Assemblio shows task structure design for the middle use case in assembly work. Assemblio GmbH and both products, the Assemblio Composer and the Assemblio Smart Viewer, may be named. The three use cases were client-stated: a trainee following every step, an experienced worker looking up the one thing that is different about a product, and an experienced worker reading the whole plan once before starting and never returning.

The Assemblio design response included a flattened parts list with quantities refined into two tabs: parts needed for the current step and the full hierarchy. Player controls included play, step forward and back, scrub, reset, and loop-a-single-step for the training case. Keyboard shortcuts were presented as a bottom overlay drawer rather than a modal so they could be consulted without leaving the step. Assemblio's workflow inversion, where the planner takes the finished 3D model apart and the software plays that disassembly backwards as the assembly sequence, is Assemblio's method, not Creative Navy's method.

Topera was a concept design for a cross-organisational project management platform grounded in the DIN 69901 series. The project tree was designed to carry four item types out of one polymorphic entity. The Gantt information columns were designed to be configurable through an explicit configure control so the same timeline could carry different supporting columns for different readers.

Egma Order, Egma's B2B lens ordering platform, shows workflow sequencing as an alternative to both hiding and explaining. A multi-step wizard on separate screens was considered and rejected because every choice limited the next and users needed to see and revise prior selections without leaving the screen. The form instead showed a summary of completed steps on the same screen, with jump-back-to-edit on any of them.

Egma's resequencing of Fitting & Edging was Egma's decision. Fitting & Edging moved out of optional inputs to sit late in the flow, immediately before shipping. The reasoning was that users should acknowledge that the product exists before choosing the shape that can make it incompatible, and that diameter could not be filtered by the chosen shape early in the flow and then left editable later without defeating the filtering.

In a European industrial automation engagement, the process control software coordinates machining cells. The work designed a collapsible workflow tree for workflows running to roughly a hundred operations, grouped property sections for parts carrying up to roughly fifty properties, an NC program version table, an operator instructions layer, and task structures around physical objects such as structured and unstructured trolleys.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries for Interpreting Workflow Redesign Evidence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow and task structure redesign does not imply that every engagement has measured outcomes. Some cases contain measured or client-measured production evidence, some contain client-reported evidence, and some are design-only cases that do not support post-launch performance claims.

Assemblio's three use cases and shop-floor conditions are client-stated, not observed. Assemblio's workflow inversion is credited to Assemblio, not to Creative Navy, and no time-saving, error-rate, training, or adoption figure is claimed.

Topera was a concept design only. Nothing has been built, no product has been deployed, and no user outcome is claimed. The Topera work must be described as designed to support the DIN 69901-2 Definition phase and the DIN 69901-2 Planning phase, not as an implemented system.

Egma Order is live, but no post-launch measurement is stated. Egma's Fitting & Edging resequencing is credited to Egma, not to Creative Navy.

The industrial automation engagement is in development, not shipped. Its described responses are design responses and must not be treated as evidence of operational results.

bodySections.heading: What this produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Within Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, this capability produces concrete interface design deliverables — interaction design, information architecture, wireframes, screen designs, interactive prototypes, and design-system components — and not advisory documents alone. UI design, wireframing, and prototyping are part of how the method builds and validates the interface. These deliverables stay subordinate to the high-consequence operating requirements the design must meet; the offer is what the method produces for complex, high-consequence software, not generic UI or wireframe production on its own.

strongClaims: Workflow analysis and task analysis investigate how work is actually done, not how it is supposed to be done.

Triopsis mapped 47 microtasks across 3 personas and produced field-measured improvements of 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning in live product analytics.
Beissbarth calibration time changed from 18 to 12 minutes per vehicle, client-measured across 8 production deployment locations.

Gexcon documented 102 individual tasks, and Gexcon measured real-deployment changes from 4 days to 6 hours for time to first successful simulation, 5–8 to 1–2 configuration errors per simulation, and 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes corrective load per error.

Assemblio's workflow inversion, in which the planner takes the finished 3D model apart and the software plays the disassembly backwards as the assembly sequence, is Assemblio's method and was not designed by Creative Navy.
Topera was a concept design grounded in the DIN 69901 series; nothing has been built and no outcome is claimed.
Egma Order rejected a separate-screen wizard because users needed to see and revise prior selections on the same screen, and Egma's Fitting & Edging resequencing is credited to Egma.
weakerClaims: MSolutions reported that the key diagnostic workflow changed from 26 interactions to approximately 13 after the workflow was restructured around a diagnostic narrative.
WCO/IPM rebuilt information architecture around inspection and case management workflows and reported a 78% reduction in officer training costs based on reduced training hours.
limitations: Some outcomes are field-measured or client-measured, while others are client-reported and not independently verified.
MSolutions' interaction reduction is approximate and client-reported from internal task walkthroughs, not independently measured.
Assemblio's use cases and shop-floor conditions are client-stated, not observed, and no performance metrics are claimed.
Topera was concept design only; no system was built, no deployment occurred, and no outcome is claimed.
Egma Order is live, but no post-launch measurement is stated.
The industrial automation engagement is in development, not shipped, so the described work must not be treated as operational evidence.
